name: Glycopyrrolate (oral)

lead: Oral glycopyrrolate is a prescription pill used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed.

It blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, which reduces sweat and saliva, and it does not cross into the brain easily. Dermatology sources list it among tablets used for hyperhidrosis, and reference works note oral and topical forms for gustatory and generalised sweating. Registered studies of the oral form for sweating are few and small.

paras: It is taken as a tablet under medical direction, and the drying effect is felt within days. It is often used for sweating that covers more than one area, such as the whole body.
Dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision and reduced sweating leading to heat prostration are listed. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Oral glycopyrrolate is used off-label for excessive sweating, and some users take it to keep skin and clothing dry and look more composed. It blocks the signal that tells sweat glands to work, so less sweat reaches skin and clothes. Registered studies of the oral form for sweating are few and small.

lead: Glycopyrrolate, also called glycopyrronium bromide, is a synthetic quaternary-ammonium muscarinic anticholinergic that acts mainly outside the brain. It is given by mouth, injection, topically or by inhalation and has been used since 1961, first for peptic ulcer [1].

In appearance-related discussion, oral glycopyrrolate is mentioned for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis). Reference works state that oral and topical forms have been used for gustatory and generalised sweating [1]. The FDA's 2018 approval concerned a separate topical product, glycopyrronium tosylate, for underarm sweating [1]. Published evidence for oral use in hyperhidrosis found here is limited to a small number of registered studies, and the injectable US label lists anaesthesia and peptic ulcer indications rather than sweating [2].

paras: Authorised uses vary by formulation and country. Reported uses include peptic ulcer, reducing secretions before anaesthesia (since 1975), drooling, and COPD in inhaled form [1][2]. Use for hyperhidrosis by mouth is described in reference works [1], and dermatology reviews group glycopyrrolate with propantheline and oxybutynin as oral anticholinergics used for focal and generalised sweating [3].

Glycopyrrolate competitively blocks muscarinic receptors, inhibiting cholinergic transmission, which reduces sweat and salivary secretion. Being quaternary, it crosses the blood-brain barrier and placenta less readily than atropine [1]. About 85 percent is excreted by the kidneys [1].

Common effects listed include dry mouth, constipation, urinary hesitancy or retention, blurred vision, tachycardia, flushing and headache [1][2]. The label warns of acute angle-closure glaucoma in susceptible patients, drowsiness or blurred vision, and heat prostration because of decreased sweating [2].

A registered study of glycopyrrolate for antidepressant-induced excessive sweating was terminated after enrolling 5 participants [4]. A phase 2 dose-ranging study in 198 people with axillary hyperhidrosis has been registered [5]. Most large published trials of glycopyrrolate concern COPD inhalers, anaesthesia and Parkinson's disease drooling, not appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Intravenous use before surgery to reduce secretions begins [1].
FDA approves a topical glycopyrronium product for axillary hyperhidrosis [1].
